strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and interesting empirical motivation (Fig 2) showing that a trained DRL policy can still identify bad actions under distribution shift even though its ranking of good actions among the remaining ones degrades. This observation nicely motivates the pruning+selection decomposition.

The idea of decoupling pruning and selection policies, combined with meta-learning (MAML) for the pruning/selection initialization and lightweight finetuning of only the selection policy at test time, is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural contribution for online 3D-BPP adaptation.

The experimental protocol covers both discrete and continuous environments, and both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets, which is a relatively comprehensive evaluation setup compared to prior online 3D-BPP work.
An ablation study (ASAP w/o MAML, ASAP w/o Decouple) is included to try to isolate the individual contribution of the two design choices (decoupling vs. meta-learning initialization).
weaknesses: Several broken cross-references remain in the manuscript ('details in ??', 'see in ??' for preliminary pruning experiments) — a section that is explicitly referenced to justify the pruning design (the preliminary MCTS pruning experiment) is entirely missing from the paper as submitted, making a core motivating claim unverifiable.

The reported performance gains, while consistently positive, are often very small in absolute terms (e.g., adaptation improvements of 0.1%-0.9% on ID datasets, generalization gains of 1-3 percentage points over baselines), and no statistical significance testing, variance, or confidence intervals are reported across the 100 sampled distributions per dataset, making it hard to assess whether the improvements are robust or within noise.

The MAML-based training procedure requires access to multiple training distributions p_i(I) sampled during meta-training (Algorithm 1), but the paper's dataset description only describes fixed item-size ranges without much detail on how many/which distributions are actually used to construct the meta-training task distribution — this is an important reproducibility gap.

The comparison baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) are also 'adapted' via finetuning in the experiments, but the finetuning procedure for baselines is not described in detail (e.g., is it done with the same MAML procedure or vanilla gradient descent?); if baselines are finetuned differently, the comparison of 'adaptation improvement' may not be entirely fair.

The two-phase training procedure (Section IV-A) and the exact interaction of pruning-policy gradient (Eq. 2, using type-I/type-II error terminology quite loosely rather than formally) is described somewhat informally; the practical mechanics of how pruned/selection policies co-train without collapsing (mentioned qualitatively as 'interference') lack a rigorous or quantitative treatment.

There is no analysis of computational overhead of running two networks (pruning + selection) versus a single-policy baseline, which is relevant to claims about efficiency and practicality of the adaptation phase.

The datasets used are all synthetic parametric families varying primarily in item-size range, and 'OOD' is defined merely as a wider/shifted range of the same distribution family (uniform box sizes) rather than a qualitatively different or realistic distribution shift (e.g., real warehouse item statistics), which limits how far the generalization/adaptation claims extend to real-world settings.

The improvement magnitudes for adaptation (e.g., 0.3% on Default dataset explained away as 'ASAP uses its item set to generate training instances') suggest a somewhat post-hoc explanation of underwhelming results rather than a principled discussion of when/why the method's adaptation benefit is limited.

Related work discussion of GOPT is dismissed with a brief unverified claim ('altering container size is akin to normalizing container size and altering incoming item size') without empirical comparison to substantiate that this narrows GOPT's applicability relative to ASAP's stated scope.

strengths: The paper tackles an under-explored aspect of online 3D-BPP (rapid test-time adaptation combined with generalization), motivated by a plausible empirical observation that pruning of the action space appears distribution-agnostic while fine-grained ranking is distribution-specific.

The proposed pruning+selection decomposition combined with MAML-based initialization and selection-only finetuning is a reasonably intuitive design, and the two-phase training scheme is clearly described at a conceptual level.

Experiments span both discrete and continuous action spaces and cover multiple in-distribution and out-of-distribution item-size regimes, and an ablation (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple) is provided to isolate the contribution of each proposed component.
Comparisons are made against several recent, relevant baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) under a supposedly consistent training/adaptation budget.
weaknesses: The paper's central motivating evidence is missing from the manuscript: the key MCTS pruned-vs-full-action-set experiment that is used to justify the entire pruning/selection decomposition is only referenced via broken cross-references ('see in ??', 'details in ??') and no actual figure/table of these results is shown. This is not a cosmetic issue -- it is the core empirical justification for the architecture and cannot be verified.

Reported improvements from adaptation and generalization are frequently very small (often 0.1%-1% Uti, sometimes even negative for baselines), yet no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests (across seeds/distributions) are reported anywhere in Tables I-II, making it impossible to assess whether the claimed gains are reliable or within noise.

The notion of 'distribution shift' / generalization tested is quite narrow: only the range of item cuboid side lengths is varied (Small/Medium/Large/Default/OOD), while container size is fixed (L=W=H=20) across all experiments and no shape-correlation, non-uniform, or structurally different distributions are tested. This limits the generality of the generalization/adaptation claims made in the abstract and title ('generalizable').

The extra computational overhead of running two policies (pruning + selection) at both training and inference time relative to single-policy baselines is never quantified (wall-clock time, FLOPs, or parameter count), which is important for judging practical significance, especially since 'rapid adaptation' is a central claimed benefit.

The MAML-based joint training procedure for two interacting/decoupled policies is described only at a high level (Algorithm 1 is the vanilla MAML loop and it's unclear how exactly gradients/adaptation steps are computed jointly for the pruning and selection networks when they are trained via each other's rollouts); important implementation details (e.g., how advantage estimates are computed for the pruning policy during meta-training, learning-rate schedules, number of MAML inner steps) are largely omitted, hurting reproducibility.

No explicit Limitations section exists (only a one-line 'future work' statement in the conclusion), and no discussion of failure cases, worst-case behavior, or scenarios where the pruning policy might discard genuinely valuable actions (type II error) beyond a brief conceptual mention.

The fairness of the baseline comparison is questionable: PCT, AR2L, and GOPT were not originally designed with the same finetuning/adaptation protocol used here, and it is unclear whether the chosen adaptation procedure (200 batches, 1/300 of training data) is well-tuned for these baselines or only for ASAP, which could bias the reported adaptation gaps in ASAP's favor.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated empirical phenomenon (Section III.B) — that a trained DRL policy's pruning-quality of actions is more robust to distribution shift than its fine-grained ranking of remaining actions — and uses this insight to justify the pruning/selection decomposition, giving the method a clear mechanistic rationale rather than being purely heuristic.

The problem framing is useful and underexplored: most prior online 3D-BPP work (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) targets generalization only, while this paper explicitly also targets rapid test-time adaptation, which is practically relevant (e.g., changing item distributions in logistics).

The two-phase training scheme (MAML-based joint initialization followed by decoupled fine-tuning, then selection-only online adaptation) is a sensible design that leverages the asymmetry between the two sub-policies (pruning being more distribution-agnostic, selection being more domain-specific).

The empirical evaluation is fairly extensive, covering both discrete and continuous action spaces, multiple in-distribution and out-of-distribution item-size subsets, and includes an ablation study (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple) that helps isolate the contribution of each proposed component.

Comparisons against recent, relevant baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) under a consistent training/adaptation budget give some confidence that the reported gains are not simply due to unequal computational resources.
weaknesses: The manuscript contains multiple broken cross-references (literal '??' in Section III.A and III.B, e.g., 'details in ??', 'preliminary experiments (see in ??)'), indicating missing figures/appendix content that is referenced but not provided, which hampers verification of some of the central motivating claims (e.g., the MCTS pruning experiment results are never actually shown).

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in Tables I and II, despite results being aggregated over randomly sampled distributions/instances; many reported improvements (e.g., +0.1–0.3% utilization) are numerically small enough that their statistical significance cannot be assessed without such information.

Despite adaptation speed/efficiency being a central motivation of the paper, no wall-clock time, sample-efficiency curves, or computational overhead comparison (e.g., MAML inner-loop rollouts cost) between ASAP and baselines during adaptation is provided — only utilization before/after a fixed number of finetuning batches is shown, which does not fully substantiate the 'rapid adaptation' claim relative to baselines under equal compute/time.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations or discussion section (the conclusion is only a few sentences); important limitations such as the added architectural/training complexity of maintaining two coupled policies, sensitivity to MAML hyperparameters (α, β, number of meta-tasks), or behavior under very large/complex OOD shifts are not discussed.

Some analysis is based on informal visual comparison (Figure 2) of 'Optimal Frequency' vs 'Policy-Induced Frequency' curves rather than a quantitative statistical test, which is a soft form of evidence for the central hypothesis motivating the architecture.

The scope is restricted to regular (cuboid) online 3D-BPP with square containers of fixed size; while this is reasonably scoped and acknowledged, it somewhat limits the generality of claims about 'generalizable online bin packing' relative to irregular-shape or variable-container settings addressed by some related work.

Reproducibility could be strengthened: exact MAML hyperparameters (α, β, number of inner/outer steps, number of sampled distributions per batch) and network/training details for GAT+ACKTR backbone are not fully specified in the main text, and no code/data release is mentioned.

strengths: The paper is motivated by careful, well-designed preliminary experiments (MCTS-based estimation of 'optimal' action frequencies vs. policy-induced frequencies) that empirically justify the core design conjecture that identifying promising actions (proposal) generalizes better across distributions than selecting the single best action (selection). This gives the architectural choice non-trivial empirical grounding rather than being purely intuition-driven.

The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive: both discrete and continuous action spaces, four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution dataset variants, comparisons against multiple recent SOTA baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) and an MCTS oracle upper bound, plus ablations (w/o Decouple, w/o MAML) and a hyperparameter sensitivity study (choice of k) in the appendix.

The paper explicitly targets a genuinely under-explored problem—fast online adaptation to distribution shift in 3D bin packing—rather than just static generalization, which is a reasonable and practically motivated contribution given deployment scenarios like changing product distributions.

Time-cost analysis (Table 5, Figure 9) is a nice addition, showing the proposed two-phase/meta-learning training and decoupled inference do not introduce a prohibitive overhead relative to baselines, and clarifies why adaptation (rather than full retraining) is valuable given the dominant simulation cost.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details are provided (hyperparameters, dataset generation procedure, network architecture, hardware), and an appendix with additional MCTS experiments and sensitivity analysis strengthens confidence in the claims.
weaknesses: The reported performance improvements are numerically small in many cases (often 0.2%–0.9% utilization improvement from adaptation, and 1.3%-3.3% for generalization over baselines), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., variance across the 3 random seeds mentioned in Table 4) or confidence intervals are reported, making it hard to assess whether the gains are robust or within noise.

The core architectural idea (decompose decision-making into a coarse pruning/proposal step and a finer selection step, à la actor-critic/hierarchical filtering) is conceptually similar to existing candidate-generation + selection paradigms (e.g., PCT's heuristic candidate generation followed by DRL selection), so the technical novelty is more incremental (adding a second learned policy for proposal, plus MAML) than fundamentally new.

The appendix directly references 'rebuttal material' (Section A.5, referring to Tables 6 and 7 as being 'in rebuttal material'), which is inconsistent with a fresh submission and raises concerns about inadvertent disclosure of review history or careless editing when repurposing content from a previous submission cycle.

The comparison methods for 'adaptation' baselines simply fine-tune the entire baseline policy with the same limited budation as ASAP's selection-only fine-tuning; it is unclear whether a fairer ablation (e.g., only fine-tuning a comparable sub-component of baseline architectures, or giving baselines equally reduced action spaces) was attempted, so the claimed superiority of 'selection-only fine-tuning' could partly reflect an apples-to-oranges comparison rather than an intrinsic advantage of the decoupled design.

The datasets are all synthetically constructed by varying item side-length ranges (e.g., {2,4,6,8,10}, {6,8,10}, etc.) drawn from the same PCT-style discretization; this is a fairly narrow notion of 'distribution shift' and 'out-of-distribution,' and results may not necessarily transfer to more realistic warehouse/logistics item distributions (e.g., correlated or non-uniform item shapes, varying container sizes, real-world SKU data).

The claimed generalization benefit of the two-policy decomposition is motivated largely by frequency-matching plots in a single specific inner setting (top-k inclusion of MCTS-optimal action); the argument that 'proposal is domain-free, selection is domain-specific' is plausible but not rigorously proven, and could be sensitive to how MCTS estimates 'optimal' probabilities (using a fixed number of simulated future sequences and a possibly imperfect DRL rollout policy), which introduces potential bias into the motivating evidence itself.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored angle for online 3D-BPP: not just cross-distribution generalization (as in prior DRL-based work such as PCT, AR2L, GOPT) but also rapid online adaptation, which the authors correctly note is 'completely overlooked by previous work.'

The motivating preliminary study (Section 3.2, detailed in Appendix A.2) using MCTS-approximated optimal action frequencies versus policy-induced frequencies is a reasonably creative diagnostic device that gives some empirical grounding for the proposal/selection decomposition, rather than motivating the architecture purely by intuition.

The experimental protocol is fairly comprehensive: both discrete and continuous action spaces, four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution subsets, ablations (w/o Decouple, w/o MAML), inference-time cost analysis, a sensitivity study on the proposal-set size k, and a training-time cost breakdown are all reported, mostly in the appendix.

The two-phase pretrain/post-train scheme with MAML initialization is a sensible engineering solution to the stated mutual-interference problem between jointly trained proposal and selection policies, and the paper is transparent about the added training-time overhead (Table 5) being modest relative to total simulation cost.
weaknesses: Reported gains are consistently small (often 0.2%-3.3% absolute Uti improvement, and adaptation gains as small as 0.1%-0.9% on several in-distribution datasets), yet no variance, standard deviation, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in Tables 1-3 or 6-7, despite the appendix stating that 3 random seeds were used. Without any measure of variability, it is impossible to judge whether the claimed improvements over PCT/AR2L/GOPT are statistically meaningful or within noise.

The 'optimal frequency' used throughout Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 to motivate the core design conjecture is itself only an MCTS-based approximation with unspecified convergence criteria (number of sampled sequences, rollout policy quality, etc.), so the central empirical justification for decoupling proposal and selection rests on a heuristic proxy rather than a rigorously verified ground truth.

The adaptation comparison may be structurally biased in ASAP's favor: by design, only a small selection policy operating over a pruned action set is fine-tuned, which trivially requires less data to show any positive movement, whereas baselines are fine-tuned over their full (larger) action space with the same limited budget (200 batches). No baseline variant with an artificially reduced/pruned action space is tested to isolate whether the adaptation gains come from the proposed proposal/selection separation specifically, or simply from a smaller effective action space during fine-tuning.

The framing of 'adaptation' as a novel contribution is somewhat narrow: it amounts to fine-tuning one sub-policy while freezing the other, which is a fairly straightforward extension once the two-policy architecture exists, rather than a fundamentally new adaptation mechanism.

Code and data are stated to be released 'upon the paper's acceptance,' meaning full reproducibility cannot be verified at submission time; combined with several unreported implementation details (e.g., exact heuristic action-generation settings beyond EMS, exact stopping criteria for MCTS sampling), independent replication would be difficult.

The improvement from MAML is inconsistent across settings (e.g., ASAP w/o Decouple sometimes matches or exceeds ASAP w/o MAML only marginally, and in some continuous in-distribution cells the ablation deltas are 0.0%), suggesting the meta-learning component's contribution is not robustly established.

Figures central to the paper's motivating argument (Figures 2, 5, 6, 7) are small, low-resolution, and hard to interpret quantitatively (no axis value call-outs, overlapping curves), which undermines the persuasiveness of the key empirical claims underlying the architecture.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and well-motivated empirical phenomenon (mismatch between DRL policy-induced action probabilities and MCTS-approximated optimal probabilities under distribution shift, while top-k inclusion of the optimal action remains high) and uses this as the basis for a clean architectural decomposition into proposal and selection policies. The preliminary experiments in Section 3.2 and detailed appendix (Figs. 4-7) provide reasonably convincing empirical support for this motivating conjecture.

The proposal/selection decomposition is a simple, generalizable idea (not tied to a specific network architecture) that naturally suggests an efficient adaptation strategy (only fine-tuning the selection policy), which is a novel contribution relative to prior generalization-focused work (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) that does not address online adaptation at all.

Experimental coverage is fairly extensive: both discrete and continuous action spaces, in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets of varying difficulty, with/without adaptation comparisons, ablations (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple), inference-time cost analysis, and a sensitivity analysis on the proposal set size k in the appendix.

Reasonable reproducibility support: hyperparameters, dataset generation procedure, and algorithmic details (MAML-based training, MCTS approximation procedure) are described in the appendix, and code/data are promised to be released upon acceptance.

The paper includes a thoughtful analysis of why adaptation matters from a computational-cost perspective (simulator cost breakdown in Figure 9), which strengthens the practical motivation for the adaptation contribution rather than just reporting utilization numbers.
weaknesses: The magnitude of the reported adaptation gains is quite small in absolute terms (mostly +0.2% to +2.3% utilization improvement over already-strong baselines), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., variance across the 3 random seeds mentioned in Table 4) is reported in the main tables, making it hard to assess whether the improvements are robust or within noise.

The MCTS-based 'Optimal Frequency' used to justify the core conjecture is itself an approximation relying on a well-trained DRL policy for rollouts, which could bias the notion of 'optimal' toward actions already favored by DRL-style reasoning; this circularity is not discussed as a potential confound.

The appendix text explicitly references 'Table 6 and Table 7 in rebuttal material' language that appears to be leftover from a prior review cycle, raising minor concerns about careful proofreading/preparation of the current submission, though this does not affect scientific content.

The comparison baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) are adapted only via simple fine-tuning per the same protocol as ASAP; it is not entirely clear whether these baselines were tuned as carefully for the adaptation setting as ASAP was for its own design, since adaptation is a new problem setting not originally proposed by those papers, which could bias the comparison somewhat in ASAP's favor.

Limitations discussion is minimal (a single sentence about extending to other decision-making scenarios in the conclusion); there is no explicit discussion of failure cases, sensitivity to the pre-training/post-training split, or potential negative societal impacts.

The datasets used (uniformly random item distributions with size ranges) are relatively synthetic/simplified compared to real logistics data, and it is unclear how well the observed conjecture (proposal easier to generalize than selection) would hold under more complex, structured, or adversarial real-world distribution shifts.
